about: Two formulas, both in the subjunctive: misereátur, perdúcat, tríbuat — may He have mercy, may He bring, may He grant. The priest does not say “I absolve” here but asks that God do it; that is the grammatical difference between these prayers and sacramental absolution. The ministers have just said the first of them back at the priest in the singular: “misereátur tui… peccátis tuis… perdúcat te”. The same prayer is made twice over, once in each direction.

s01.narrative: With hands joined, the priest says over the servers and the faithful the first of two prayers for forgiveness.

s02.translation: May almighty God have mercy on you, and having forgiven your sins, bring you to life everlasting.

s04.narrative: The priest signs himself with the cross and says the second prayer — the one in which he asks for himself as well: nostrórum, nobis.

s05.translation: May the almighty and merciful Lord grant us pardon, absolution and remission of our sins.

w001.function: A subjunctive of wish: not “he had mercy” but “may he have mercy”. The whole prayer is a petition addressed to God about someone else, not a sentence passed.

w002.function: The genitive of the pronoun “you”, not the possessive adjective: misereor governs the genitive of the person pitied. The same form vestri belongs to the paradigm of “your” as well — hence the temptation to read it as a possessive, like “vestris” (w008).

w004.function: Nominative: the subject, though it comes only fourth. The prayer opens with its verb, as these formulas of blessing do.

w006.function: The participle opens an ablative absolute — a phrase standing free of the rest of the sentence: “your sins having been forgiven”.

w007.function: The subject of the ablative absolute with “dimíssis” (w006).

w008.function: Agrees with “peccátis” (w007). This is the possessive adjective, unlike “vestri” (w002) — one family of words, two different jobs.

w009.function: A second subjunctive of wish, joined to the first: may he have mercy and may he bring.

w015.function: Accusative: the first of three objects that “tríbuat” (w021) grants. All three come before the verb.

w018.function: Three nouns for three sides of forgiveness, piled up in the manner of the late-medieval absolution formulas.

w020.function: Agrees with “peccatórum” (w019). The priest says “our”, not “your”: here he counts himself in.

w021.function: A third subjunctive of wish; the verb closes the long chain of objects with which the sentence opens.

w025.function: A compound of miser (wretched) and cor (heart); the two adjectives describe God from two sides — power and pity.

w026.function: Nominative: the subject, and only at the very end of the sentence.
